It reads the next token from the current lexer state and supplies it to the consuming parser routines, which then use the value for subsequent decisions in the syntax tree.

@lstd::basic_istream::operator>>@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_istream::operator>>@k_ZNSt1.body: The overload of operator>> takes a reference to a `long` and pulls a numeric value from the supplied input stream object (`__istream_type`). It parses characters, converts them to a `long`, assigns the result to the target variable, and returns the stream reference to allow further extraction chaining.

@lstd::basic_istream::read@k_ZNSt13basic.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_istream::read@k_ZNSt13basic.body: The `read` function consumes a buffer pointer and the number of bytes to read, returning a reference to the underlying input stream. It fetches data into the supplied buffer, advancing the stream’s internal position accordingly.

@lstd::basic_istream::seekg@k_ZNSt13basi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_istream::seekg@k_ZNSt13basi.body: The `seekg` function changes the stream’s current read position according to the supplied offset and direction, then returns the stream reference for fluent chaining.

@lstd::basic_istream::seekg@k_ZNSt13basi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_istream::seekg@k_ZNSt13basi.body: The function `seekg` moves the read position of a stream to a specified absolute position (`pos_type`) and returns a reference to the stream for fluent chaining. It performs bounds checking and throws if the requested position is outside the stream’s range, ensuring a consistent state before use.

@lstd::basic_istream::tellg@k_ZNSt13basi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_istream::tellg@k_ZNSt13basi.body: It returns a value of type `pos_type` that represents the current offset in the underlying stream, letting callers resume read/write operations from that point.

@lstd::basic_ofstream::basic_ofstream@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ofstream::basic_ofstream@k_.body: Creates an `ofstream`‑style stream object from a file‑name and an `openmode`. The first argument is the path string; the second indicates how the file should be opened (append, truncate, binary, etc.). The function typically allocates a stream object, calls the underlying implementation to open the file with those flags, and returns the constructed object (or a null/invalid state on failure).

@lstd::basic_ofstream::basic_ofstream@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ofstream::basic_ofstream@k_.body: The `basic_ofstream` function initializes an output stream object—allocating a buffer, associating a file descriptor, and returning a ready‑to‑write stream. It sets up the stream’s underlying file/device, configures any required flags, and ensures the stream is in a usable state for subsequent write operations.

@lstd::basic_ofstream::close@k_ZNSt14bas.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ofstream::close@k_ZNSt14bas.body: The `close()` method is responsible for gracefully releasing any allocated resources, rolling back pending state changes, and marking the object as no longer usable—essentially ensuring that after a call to `close()` no further operations can be performed on the instance and that any underlying handles (e.g. file descriptors, sockets, locks) are properly released so that the system can recover without leaking resources.

@lstd::basic_ofstream::is_open@k_ZNSt14b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ofstream::is_open@k_ZNSt14b.body: Returns true when the resource is currently open; returns false otherwise.

@lstd::basic_ofstream::open@k_ZNSt14basi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ofstream::open@k_ZNSt14basi.body: The `open` function opens a file specified by the path string using the requested `ios_base::openmode`. It resolves errors, sets up necessary flags, and returns status while safeguarding against invalid modes and I/O failures.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The overloaded `operator<<` accepts a function‑pointer manipulator (e.g., `std::endl`, `std::flush`), invokes it with the current stream and returns that stream so calls can be chained. It essentially forwards the manipulator to the underlying stream object without altering its internal state beyond what the manipulator does.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The operator<< overload simply forwards an insertion operation to the underlying stream object, returning a reference to that stream type so calls can be chained. It accepts a reference to an ios_base-derived object and yields a reference to the internal stream type (`__ostream_type`) that actually performs the output.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The overload takes a pointer to a stream buffer (typically a `std::streambuf`) and inserts it into the stream, returning a reference to the stream so calls can be chained. It essentially forwards the buffer into the output stream, enabling the usual `cout << value` syntax for objects that provide this operator.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The operator inserts a single‑character representation of the boolean value into the stream: it outputs “1” for true and “0” for false. It returns the stream reference so calls can be chained, enabling syntax like `os << true << false`. It’s typically defined in a header to allow bool values to be written with the usual stream interface.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The overload inserts the double value into the stream and returns a reference to that stream so calls can be chained. It accepts the value by value and streams it using the stream’s insertion logic (e.g., converting to a string‑like representation). The function is expected to work with any stream type that meets the `__ostream_type` concept, enabling use in templated code.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The overload writes the supplied `float` value into the stream object and returns a reference to that stream, enabling further chained insertions.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: Inserts the supplied integer into the stream’s buffer, updates the stream state, and returns a reference to that same stream for further chaining.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The overload streams an unsigned integer value into the custom `__ostream_type`, emitting the value as text and returning the stream reference for chaining.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The overload inserts a 64‑bit integer into a stream and returns the stream reference so that the call can be chained; it writes the value in the usual textual format (decimal) and leaves the stream in a usable state for subsequent output operations.

@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::operator<<@k_ZNSt1.body: The `operator<<` overload inserts an `unsigned long` value into an output stream, returning the stream reference so that calls can be chained. It simply writes the numeric value in its usual textual representation, allowing callers to stream‐output that value just as they would any other type.

@lstd::basic_ostream::put@k_ZNSt13basic_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::put@k_ZNSt13basic_.body: The `put` function inserts a single character (of type `char_type`) into the output stream and returns a reference to the stream object (`__ostream_type &`). This allows chaining of consecutive output calls in the same statement.

@lstd::basic_ostream::write@k_ZNSt13basi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_ostream::write@k_ZNSt13basi.body: The `write` function forwards a raw character buffer to the underlying stream's own `write` routine, returning the stream reference to enable chaining. It performs only basic validity checks (e.g., non‑null pointer and size > 0) before delegating; any I/O error handling is left to the caller.

@lstd::basic_streambuf::pubseekoff@k_ZNS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_streambuf::pubseekoff@k_ZNS.body: pubseekoff moves the internal read/write pointer of the stream’s buffer by a given offset relative to a seek base (beginning, current or end) and returns the resulting absolute position. It validates bounds against the buffer size, raises an error on overflow, and honours the open mode to decide whether the move is allowed.

@lstd::basic_string_view::at@k_ZNKSt17ba.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::at@k_ZNKSt17ba.body: The `at` member returns the character at the requested index. It is a `const` function, so it does not modify the object. Internally it delegates to the underlying `view_` container’s `at` method, returning the value at position `pos`. It simply provides bounds‑checked access to the element stored at that position.

@lstd::basic_string_view::back@k_ZNKSt17.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::back@k_ZNKSt17.body: Returns a const reference to the element at the very end of the underlying container, guaranteeing the element exists (otherwise a logic error would be thrown).

@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.body: `basic_string_view` wraps a raw character pointer into a lightweight `string_view` that merely references the underlying buffer without copying. It is used throughout the code to construct views of substrings (e.g., appending offsets like `arg.c_str() + COMPARE.length()`), allowing efficient string manipulation.

@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.body: The function `basic_string_view` constructs a lightweight view of a character buffer by taking a pointer to the buffer and its size. It returns a `string_view` object that internally stores that raw pointer and length; no copy of the underlying data occurs. The routine is invoked in many places in the codebase to convert C‑style strings, literals, or portions of larger buffers into `string_view` objects used throughout the utilities—for example, turning a single character into a view, slicing a dependency string, trimming suffixes from a path, or creating formatted text fragments.

@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.body: This helper constructs a non‑owning view of a string‑like object. It takes an already‑existing `basic_string_view` reference and returns a new view that references the same underlying data without copying characters. The result is a lightweight, read‑only view that can be used wherever a string slice is needed.

@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::basic_string_v.body: A single call to `basic_string_view()` produces a `string_view` (a lightweight non‑owning view of a string). The function is used throughout the project to convert ordinary strings or string‑like objects into the `string_view` type that the `cm::` helpers use for efficient string handling. It accepts an optional source string; when `nullptr` or an empty input is supplied, it returns an empty `string_view`. This utility is invoked in several places—creating views from raw C‑strings, extracting a view from a `cmString` object, and when registering values with `Makefile::AddDefinition`—making it the central point for string‑to‑view conversions in the codebase.

@lstd::basic_string_view::begin@k_ZNKSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::begin@k_ZNKSt1.body: The `begin()` member simply returns a `const_iterator` that points to the first element of the string’s internal `view_` container. It’s declared `const noexcept`, guaranteeing no throw and that the object cannot be modified. The function is invoked in several helper routines (e.g., appending or reserving) where callers need an iterator starting at the string’s beginning.

@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.body: The `compare` function takes a pointer to a character sequence and returns an `int` result—typically indicating the relative order (e.g., negative if the first sequence is less, zero if equal, positive if greater). It performs the comparison without modifying the data, preserving const‑correctness.

@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.body: The function performs a lexicographic comparison between the current string view and the one supplied in the argument. It returns an integer: zero if the two views are equal, a negative value if the current view precedes the argument, and a positive value otherwise. The comparison is delegated to the underlying `string_view::compare` implementation that operates on the underlying character sequence according to the supplied `_Traits`.

@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.body: The function performs a lexicographic comparison: it takes a start index and a length, then compares the requested substring of the current string against the supplied string pointer; the result is an integer (negative, zero, or positive) indicating whether the substring is less than, equal to, or greater than the other string.

@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.body: The `compare` member compares a substring of the current string—starting at `pos1` for `count1` characters—against a supplied C‑string `s` (up to `count2` characters). It returns a negative value if this substring is lexicographically less than `s`, zero if equal, and a positive value otherwise. If either index or length exceeds bounds, the function would normally throw or assert a bounds‑error.

@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.body:
The `compare` function performs a lexicographic comparison between a substring of the current string view and another string view. It takes three parameters:

1. **`pos`** – the starting index of the substring to compare.  
2. **`count`** – the length of that substring.  
3. **`rhs`** – the string view to compare against.

The function returns an `int`:

* `0` if the two sequences are equal,  
* a negative value if the substring is lexicographically less than `rhs`,  
* a positive value if it is greater.

Internally it executes a simple byte‑by‑byte comparison over the requested range, mirroring the semantics of `std::basic_string_view::compare`.

@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::compare@k_ZNKS.body: The `compare` function performs a lexicographic comparison of two substrings taken from two `basic_string_view` objects. It takes the start positions and lengths of the portions to compare, and returns an integer in the same style as `std::string::compare`: a negative value if the first substring is less than the second, zero if they are equal, and a positive value otherwise. This helper is used in `cmString.hxx` to delegate the actual string‑view comparison to the underlying view’s `compare` method.

@lstd::basic_string_view::data@k_ZNKSt17.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::data@k_ZNKSt17.body: The `data` member returns a raw pointer to the underlying character array of the string object. Because the method is `const` and marked `noexcept`, callers can safely use the returned pointer without fearing modification of the object or unexpected exceptions. In the shown snippets, it is employed to obtain pointers to specific slices of the internal buffer (`text.data() + i`, `+ l`) and to copy chunks into other string instances (`append(v.data(), v.size())`). Use the pointer only while the owning string remains alive, and avoid writing through it because the method promises no modification of the underlying data.

@lstd::basic_string_view::empty@k_ZNKSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::empty@k_ZNKSt1.body: The `empty()` function is a simple, const member that returns a boolean indicating whether the underlying string view contains any characters. It’s employed throughout the codebase to guard further logic that expects a non‑empty string—e.g., before accessing `front()` or `back()` or before parsing arguments that begin with a dash. This quick check prevents out‑of‑bounds errors and allows callers to short‑circu‑tate entire logic paths when the string is in fact empty.

@lstd::basic_string_view::end@k_ZNKSt17b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::end@k_ZNKSt17b.body: It returns a `const_iterator` that points at the first position past the last character of the underlying view. The method is marked `noexcept` and does not modify any internal state; it simply forwards the call to the stored view’s own `end()` function, which yields an iterator representing the logical end of the sequence. This iterator is then used by callers (e.g. in `append`, `substr`, etc.) to demarcate the boundary of the string without changing the original data.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find@k_ZNKSt17.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find@k_ZNKSt17.body: It scans the underlying view for the first occurrence of a sequence of characters that starts at a supplied offset and is no longer than a supplied count. The function returns the position where that sequence begins within the string, or a special value indicating that no match was found.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find@k_ZNKSt17.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find@k_ZNKSt17.body: The `find` member simply scans the underlying character buffer starting at an optional offset and reports the offset where the requested sub‑sequence first appears; if the sequence is absent it returns the sentinel `size_type(-1)` (the usual “not found” marker). This behavior is relied on by several modules for quick substring checks without mutating the view.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_not.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_not.body: The `find_first_not_of` routine scans a block of characters starting at a supplied offset and returns the index of the first element that does **not** belong to a given character set. It returns the position relative to the beginning of the array; if every examined character belongs to the set, the function reports the size of the sequence (commonly used as an “npos” sentinel). The implementation performs a straightforward linear scan using raw pointers for speed, and is typically invoked by higher‑level string utilities such as the `cmString` view search helpers.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_not.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_not.body:
`find_first_not_of` scans a view of a string for the first character that is **not** in a given set of characters.  
It accepts a `basic_string_view` (the string to search) and a starting index `pos`.  
The function returns the index of that first non‑matching character, or `static_cast<size_type>(-1)` (typically `string_view::npos`) if none is found.  
In the surrounding code it’s used to locate the next separator in parsing routines and to skip over trailing delimiters when parsing input streams.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_of@.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_of@.body: find_first_of scans a string view starting at a given offset for at most count characters, returning the index of the first encountered character that matches any of the characters supplied in the input buffer; if no such character is found it returns the special sentinel (often npos). It is implemented as a thin wrapper that forwards the request to the underlying view (as seen in the call from cmString::view_).

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_of@.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_first_of@.body: The function `find_first_of` scans a string view for the first character that belongs to a supplied set of characters. It starts searching at a given index and returns that position, or an “npos” sentinel if none of the specified characters appears.  It’s employed in the codebase to locate delimiters such as separators or any specific pattern strings, as shown in the three call sites.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_not_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_not_.body: The function scans a string in reverse order, starting at the supplied index, and returns the index of the first character that is not one of the characters in the provided set. If no such character exists before the start index, it returns an indicator (e.g., npos).

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_not_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_not_.body: The function scans the string view backward starting at the supplied position. It returns the index of the first character that is not any of the characters contained in the argument string view, or `npos` if no such character exists.

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_of@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_of@k.body: find_last_of searches a character array for the last occurrence of any character from a given set within a specified range and returns that index (or npos if none found).

@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_of@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::find_last_of@k.body: The `find_last_of` member searches the view from the end, returning the index of the first character encountered that matches any character in the supplied `basic_string_view`. If no match exists, it returns `npos`.

@lstd::basic_string_view::front@k_ZNKSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::front@k_ZNKSt1.body: front() returns the first character of the internal string view (the underlying string view’s front() method). It’s a const noexcept function that simply forwards the call to the internal view and returns that character.

@lstd::basic_string_view::length@k_ZNKSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::length@k_ZNKSt.body: The `length()` member simply returns the size of the internally stored view (via `this->view_.length()`), and is marked `const noexcept` to guarantee no state changes or exceptions.

@lstd::basic_string_view::operator=@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::operator=@k_ZN.body: Assigns an existing `basic_string_view` from another, copying its internal pointer and length. It accepts a const reference to the source view, performs no allocation or copying of the string data itself, and returns a reference to the left‑hand side (`*this`) for chaining. The operation is noexcept in that it never throws and only works when the template parameters match; otherwise the code fails to compile.

@lstd::basic_string_view::operator[]@k_Z.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::operator[]@k_Z.body: Returns a const reference to the element at the requested index, so the returned reference cannot modify the stored value.

@lstd::basic_string_view::rbegin@k_ZNKSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::rbegin@k_ZNKSt.body: Returns a `const_reverse_iterator` that points to the first element of the underlying view, allowing read‑only reverse traversal of the string.

@lstd::basic_string_view::rend@k_ZNKSt17.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::rend@k_ZNKSt17.body: The `rend()` member simply forwards the underlying view’s `rend()` call – it returns a `const_reverse_iterator` that points past the first element when the container is viewed in reverse order. The function is `const` and `noexcept`, meaning it guarantees no modification of the object and will never throw.

@lstd::basic_string_view::rfind@k_ZNKSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::rfind@k_ZNKSt1.body:
`rfind` performs a right‑to‑left search for a character sequence in a string view.  
It scans the view starting from the supplied `pos` offset, examining at most `count` characters, and returns the index of the last matching occurrence; if none is found it returns the sentinel value `size_type::npos`. The function is invoked on a view object (e.g., `this->view_`) to locate a substring within that view.

@lstd::basic_string_view::rfind@k_ZNKSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::rfind@k_ZNKSt1.body: The `rfind` function performs a reverse search in a string view: given a view `v` and a starting position `pos`, it scans backward from `pos` to locate the first occurrence of `v` and returns its index (or `npos` if none is found). It’s used throughout the code to test whether a substring appears at a given position, often to validate prefixes or suffixes in path handling logic.

@lstd::basic_string_view::size@k_ZNKSt17.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::size@k_ZNKSt17.body: The `size()` member simply returns the length of the current string view. It’s a `const noexcept` accessor that retrieves `view_.size()` and is invoked whenever the code needs to know the string’s current length – for example, to pre‑allocate space in `reserve` (see line 415), to know how many bytes to copy in `append` (lines 417‑470), and in the constructor to compute the new total length. The function is trivial, side‑effect‑free and designed for maximum performance and safety.

@lstd::basic_string_view::substr@k_ZNKSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::basic_string_view::substr@k_ZNKSt.body: The `substr(size_type pos, size_type n)` member of `basic_string_view` creates a new view that represents a contiguous slice of the underlying character sequence. It does not copy any characters; instead it simply adjusts the internal pointer and length to point at the requested segment. When `pos + n` exceeds the original view’s length, the returned view will cover only the characters that exist up to the end of the source. The function does not perform bounds checking beyond the usual sanity checks performed by the container’s own mechanisms; it is the caller’s responsibility to avoid out‑of‑range arguments. It returns a view that can be used directly in subsequent operations such as concatenation (`cmStrCat`), further slicing (`substr` again), or conversion to `std::string` when an actual copy is required.

@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginRAT0__T_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginRAT0__T_.body: The `begin` template produces an iterator that points to the first element of a static array. It allows code that works with generic ranges to consume the array without knowing its size at run‑time, enabling loops such as `for(auto it = std::begin(arr); it != std::end(arr); ++it)` to iterate over the entire collection.

@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginRKSt8valarrayIT_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginRKSt8valarrayIT_.body: Provides a const pointer to the first element of the underlying storage of a `valarray`. The returned pointer can be used as a “begin” iterator for sequential traversal, and is valid only when the array is non‑empty (otherwise it points at the array’s internal buffer).

@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginRSt8valarrayIT_E.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginRSt8valarrayIT_E.body: This template defines a utility called `begin` that accepts a `valarray<_Tp>` instance and returns a raw pointer (`_Tp*`) pointing at the array’s first element. The function is intended to provide an iterator‑like start point for range‑based algorithms or loops that operate on the underlying storage of a `valarray`. It simply forwards the address of the first element of the container without copying or bounds checking.

@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginSt16initializer_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::begin@k_ZSt5beginSt16initializer_.body: The `begin` overload simply returns a pointer to the first element of an `initializer_list` instance. It lets the list participate in standard iterator‑based algorithms (range‑based `for`, copy/move utilities, etc.) by exposing the underlying storage address while still respecting const‑correctness and noexcept guarantees.

@lstd::begin@kc3std::begin.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::begin@kc3std::begin.body: The `begin` function template is a small utility that simply forwards to the underlying container’s `begin` to produce an iterator pointing at the first element of a container. It works uniformly for any type that exposes a `begin()` member or an overload in its namespace, allowing code to use `begin(container)` in generic algorithms like `std::transform`, `std::find`, and `std::distance`.

@lstd::boolalpha@k_ZSt9boolalphaRSt8ios_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::boolalpha@k_ZSt9boolalphaRSt8ios_.body: The function `boolalpha` is a stream‑manipulator that operates on an `ios_base` object. When invoked, it adjusts (or queries) a boolean flag in the stream’s internal state—often used to enable or disable a particular output format or parsing mode. After performing its operation, it returns the modified stream object so that the stream can be chained with other manipulators (`<<`).

@lstd::chrono::_V2::steady_clock::now@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::chrono::_V2::steady_clock::now@k_.body: The function `now` returns the current point in time represented as a `time_point`. It is a thin wrapper around `std::chrono::steady_clock::now()`, providing a monotonic, thread‑safe timestamp that callers use to record start times or compute elapsed durations.

@lstd::chrono::_V2::system_clock::now@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::chrono::_V2::system_clock::now@k_.body: It returns a `time_point` representing the current instant, essentially a thin wrapper around `std::chrono::system_clock::now()`.

@lstd::chrono::duration::count@k_ZNKSt6c.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::chrono::duration::count@k_ZNKSt6c.body: `count()` simply returns the internal numeric value stored in the duration object (typically a 64‑bit millisecond counter). It is a read‑only accessor used wherever the code serialises or compares elapsed times.

@lstd::chrono::duration::duration@k_ZNSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::chrono::duration::duration@k_ZNSt.body: Creates a new `duration` by copying the representation of another `duration` (possibly with a different representation type or period). This constructor enables implicit conversion between compatible `duration` types.

@lstd::chrono::duration::duration@k_ZNSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::chrono::duration::duration@k_ZNSt.body: The function template simply returns a `duration` object constructed from the supplied `duration` argument, preserving its underlying representation and period type.

@lstd::chrono::duration::duration@k_ZNSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::chrono::duration::duration@k_ZNSt.body:
The `duration` template is a convenience wrapper that extracts a `std::chrono::duration` from a type that models `Rep2`.

@lstd::min@k_ZSt3minRKT_S1_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::min@k_ZSt3minRKT_S1_.body: The `min` template simply compares two values and returns a reference to the one that is smaller. It accepts the arguments as const references to avoid unnecessary copying and returns a const reference to the smaller value, keeping the original type unchanged. The implementation relies on the `<` operator being defined for the type passed in.

@lstd::move@k_ZSt4moveOT_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::move@k_ZSt4moveOT_.body: The `move` template forwards its argument by stripping any reference wrapper (`std::remove_reference<_Tp>::type`) and returns the argument as an rvalue (`&&`). It is a thin wrapper that preserves value‑category without copying, enabling efficient construction of temporary objects in the surrounding code.

@lstd::move@k_ZSt4moveOT_T0_S1_T1_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::move@k_ZSt4moveOT_T0_S1_T1_.body: The `move` template performs an element‑wise move of a range of elements from a source range to a destination range under a given execution policy. It accepts an execution policy type, a source begin iterator, a source end iterator, and a destination beginning iterator. The function forwards each element from the source to the destination and returns an iterator that points to the position just after the last element written into the destination.

@lstd::move@k_ZSt4moveT_S_T0_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::move@k_ZSt4moveT_S_T0_.body: The `move` template performs a move‑semantics transfer between two instances of type `_II`, producing a result of type `_OI`. It essentially relocates data (or ownership) from the first argument to the second, returning the moved‑to value.

@lstd::next@k_ZSt4nextT_NSt15iterator_tr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::next@k_ZSt4nextT_NSt15iterator_tr.body: The `next` template increments an iterator by a given offset, returning the iterator that points to the element after that many steps. It uses `iterator_traits` to deduce the correct difference type so the call works with any iterator type that supports that operation. The snippets in *cmConditionEvaluator.cxx* show it used to move a pointer or iterator forward during various parsing stages.

@lstd::none_of@k_ZSt7none_ofOT_T0_S1_T1_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::none_of@k_ZSt7none_ofOT_T0_S1_T1_.body: This template returns a boolean indicating whether no element in the given iterator range satisfies the supplied predicate. It conditionally enables itself via an execution‑policy‑based `enable_if`, providing a compile‑time guard that the call is only valid when the policy permits the operation.

@lstd::none_of@k_ZSt7none_ofT_S_T0_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::none_of@k_ZSt7none_ofT_S_T0_.body: `none_of` is a generic helper that accepts a pair of iterators and a predicate; it scans the range and returns `true` if and only if no element in the range satisfies the predicate, otherwise `false`.

@lstd::nullopt_t::nullopt_t@k_ZNSt9nullo.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::nullopt_t::nullopt_t@k_ZNSt9nullo.body: The function takes a const reference to a `nullopt_t` instance and returns a (possibly copy‑constructed) `nullopt_t` object. It serves as a small utility to obtain a null‑safe value from an existing one, typically used when a new instance needs to be created without modifying the original.

@lstd::numeric_limits::max@k_ZNSt14numer.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::numeric_limits::max@k_ZNSt14numer.body: The `max()` function returns the maximum value representable by an `unsigned long`. It is used as a sentinel in the code to represent “no value” or “infinity” in places where a `size_t` value is required. In the two `cmFileAPICodemodel.cxx` excerpts, it’s returned when an `i.IsSystem` flag is true, otherwise zero is supplied. In `cmComputeComponentGraph.cxx` it is used to initialise or bound a size counter.

@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKNSt7__cxx1112.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKNSt7__cxx1112.body: Provides an overload that lets a `basic_string` be compared with a null‑terminated C‑string. Internally it walks the two sequences in lock‑step, returning `true` only when a length or character mismatch is detected, delegating to the string’s own comparison logic.

@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKNSt7__cxx1112.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKNSt7__cxx1112.body: This overload implements the inequality comparison for `std::basic_string`. It takes two strings (possibly of any character type, traits, or allocator) and returns `true` when their sequences of characters differ, otherwise `false`. It is a non‑member template that simply forwards to the underlying `operator==` (or `equal` function) and negates the result.

@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKSt17_Rb_tree_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKSt17_Rb_tree_.body: The operator!= returns true when any member of the two objects differs; otherwise it returns false.

@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKSt23_Rb_tree_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKSt23_Rb_tree_.body: The operator compares two objects of the same type and returns `true` when any stored member differs; otherwise it returns `false`.

@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKSt6vectorIT_T.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneRKSt6vectorIT_T.body: The operator simply returns true when any element differs or the sizes differ, otherwise false. It takes two `const vector<T,_Alloc>&` arguments and performs an element‑wise comparison to decide inequality.

@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneSt17basic_strin.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator!=@k_ZStneSt17basic_strin.body: The operator‑!= for two `basic_string_view` objects performs a lexical inequality comparison: it returns `true` when either the views differ in length or at least one character differs, otherwise `false`. The implementation typically iterates through both views in tandem, returning early if a mismatch is found or if the lengths differ. It is a `constexpr` function so it can be evaluated at compile‑time when the views are constant expressions. This operator can be used directly in `if` or `while` statements to test whether two string views are not equal.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplONSt7__cxx1112ba.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplONSt7__cxx1112ba.body: This overload of `operator+` takes an rvalue reference to a `basic_string` and a pointer to a character array, combines the two sequences, and returns a new `basic_string` containing the concatenated contents.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplONSt7__cxx1112ba.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplONSt7__cxx1112ba.body: The `operator+` template implements the string‑concatenation operator for `basic_string`. It accepts an rvalue of the left operand and a const reference to the right operand, allocates a new string that contains the first string’s contents followed by the second, and returns the newly constructed string. The implementation takes care of allocators and allocator propagation, and it is used wherever a string concatenation is required in the rest of the code.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplPKT_ONSt7__cxx11.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplPKT_ONSt7__cxx11.body: Allows you to write expressions like `"prefix" + std::string("suffix")`. This overload takes a C‑string literal on the left and an rvalue `basic_string` on the right, creates a new `basic_string` containing the literal followed by the temporary string’s contents.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplPKT_RKNSt7__cxx1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplPKT_RKNSt7__cxx1.body: The `operator+` template performs string concatenation between a raw C‑string and a `basic_string` instance, yielding a new string that contains the first argument followed by the second. It preserves allocator and character traits, constructing the result by copying the C‑string into a temporary buffer and appending the original string’s content. This helper enables seamless +‑operations in code that works with both raw and `basic_string` objects.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.body: It defines an overload of the binary `+` operator that accepts a left‑hand `basic_string` by value and a right‑hand `basic_string` by rvalue reference, returning a new string that contains the concatenated content of the two operands.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.body: The operator+ template performs a concatenation of a `basic_string` with a null‑terminated character sequence. It accepts a left‑hand `basic_string` by const‑reference and a right‑hand raw pointer, constructs a new `basic_string` that holds the joined sequence, and returns that string. It’s generally used as a convenience overload to allow expressions such as `s + "suffix"` to produce a new string without modifying the original.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.body: Adds a single character to the end of a string, returning a new string of the same type.

@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator+@k_ZStplRKNSt7__cxx1112b.body: The template defines an overload of the `operator+` for two `basic_string` arguments. It simply creates and returns a new string that is the concatenation of the two operands, allocating the result with the same allocator as the operands.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: The overload inserts a `basic_string` into a `basic_ostream`, returning the stream reference so calls can be chained. It works for any character type that satisfies the stream traits, handling both narrow and wide strings without special‑case logic. It simply forwards the string’s data to the stream’s internal buffer; complexity is linear in string size.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: This overload inserts a `std::ios_base::setiosflags` manipulator into a stream, effectively setting the stream’s formatting flags to the supplied value and returning the stream for further chaining.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: It forwards a precision manipulator to the stream object, updating that stream’s `precision` field and returning the stream reference so further chaining can continue.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: The overload takes a stream of type `basic_ostream<_CharT,_Traits>` and a `basic_string_view<_CharT,_Traits>` and writes the view’s contents to the stream by invoking `write` or `operator<<` on the underlying string. It then returns the stream reference so the call can be chained.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: The overload applies the formatting change stored in the `_Setw` argument to the stream and returns the stream reference, enabling chained calls.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: This overload sets the stream’s fill character. It takes a reference to a `basic_ostream` and a `_Setfill` manipulator object (typically created by `std::setfill`) and returns the stream reference so calls can be chained. It’s defined in `<iomanip>` to allow statements like `std::cout << std::setfill('*')` to adjust the fill character used when formatting output.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: The overload writes a C‑string to the stream: it takes a `basic_ostream<char,_Traits>` reference, copies the characters from the null‑terminated `const char*`, and returns the stream reference for chaining.

@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<<@k_ZStlsRSt13basic_ostr.body: Writes a single character into the stream, invoking the underlying `put` routine, adjusting the stream’s internal state (e.g., position, flags), and then returns the stream reference so calls can be chained.

@lstd::operator<=@k_ZStleSt17basic_strin.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<=@k_ZStleSt17basic_strin.body: The `operator<` template defines a lexical “less‑than” comparison for two `basic_string_view` objects. It takes two string‑view arguments—each parameterised by a character type and traits type—and returns `bool` indicating whether the first string is strictly lexicographically smaller than the second. The implementation typically uses the underlying string view’s `compare` function or a similar routine to perform the comparison.

@lstd::operator<@k_ZStltRKNSt7__cxx1112b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<@k_ZStltRKNSt7__cxx1112b.body: The template declares a comparison operator that takes two `basic_string` objects and returns a `bool`. It performs a lexicographical comparison between the two strings. This overload is used when strings are compared in containers or algorithms that rely on `<` for ordering, such as in sets or sorting operations.

@lstd::operator<@k_ZStltSt17basic_string.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator<@k_ZStltSt17basic_string.body: It overloads the `<` operator for two `basic_string_view` objects, performing a standard lexicographic comparison of the underlying characters and yielding a `bool` result.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqNSt15__type_ide.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqNSt15__type_ide.body: It defines an equality comparison that returns true when two `basic_string_view` objects contain identical character sequences. The operator first verifies that the two views have the same length; if they do, it then performs a sequential comparison of the underlying data until a mismatch is found or the end of the sequences is reached. If no difference is detected, the function returns true; otherwise it returns false.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqPKT_RKNSt7__cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqPKT_RKNSt7__cxx.body: The overload checks whether a C‑style string (`const _CharT *`) and a `basic_string` contain identical sequences. It first verifies that neither pointer nor string is empty, then compares lengths and finally performs a byte‑wise comparison (typically `std::char_traits<_CharT>::eq` or `std::memcmp`). If the pointer is `nullptr` the comparison yields `false`; if the string is empty it returns true only when the pointer points to a null‑terminated zero‑length string. The function is intended for use in generic string‑handling contexts where an external `operator==` is required without instantiating a string object.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKNSt7__cxx1112.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKNSt7__cxx1112.body:
This overload lets you compare a `basic_string` with a C‑style string literal.  
It is a template so it works for every character type (`char`, `wchar_t`, etc.) and allocator.  
The function takes a `const basic_string<…>&` and a `const _CharT*` and returns `true` when the two sequences contain the same characters in the same order, otherwise `false`.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKNSt7__cxx1112.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKNSt7__cxx1112.body: The `operator==` template performs a value‑wise comparison between two `std::basic_string` objects. It iterates over the underlying character containers (via iterators or `c_str()`), checking each corresponding character pair for equality. If all compared characters match and the string lengths are identical, the function returns `true`; otherwise it returns `false`. The implementation typically follows the standard library’s pattern: it first compares lengths, then a byte‑wise or character‑wise comparison of the internal buffers (often using `traits::eq`). The function is marked `constexpr` in modern implementations to allow compile‑time evaluation when the strings are constant expressions. It is `noexcept` because no allocations or throws are performed during comparison. The primary edge cases to watch for are: differing allocators (which may affect internal data layout but not comparison result), and extremely long strings where the comparison’s O(n) cost could become a performance bottleneck in tight loops. The function is designed to be efficient, avoiding unnecessary copies and using move semantics when possible.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKSt17_Rb_tree_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKSt17_Rb_tree_.body: The `operator==` overload should perform a value‑wise comparison of the two operands, returning `true` only when every relevant data member matches. It’s usually implemented as a non‑mutating member or friend function that checks each field (or a single `equal` helper) and returns the logical conjunction of those checks. In safety‑critical code it’s good to guard against self‑comparison pitfalls and use `std::memcmp` or `std::equal_range` for POD members to avoid unnecessary copying.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKSt23_Rb_tree_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKSt23_Rb_tree_.body:
It compares two instances of the same type.  
The function takes two references, one const‑qualified and one non‑qualified, and returns **true** if every member (or sub‑object) of the two arguments is equal, otherwise **false**.  
Essentially, it implements an equality check for that type.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKSt6vectorIT_T.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqRKSt6vectorIT_T.body: It takes two vector references and returns `true` if they contain the same number of elements and every element compares equal; otherwise it returns `false`.

@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqSt17basic_strin.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator==@k_ZSteqSt17basic_strin.body: It overloads the == operator for two basic_string_view objects. The implementation first checks the length of each view; if the lengths differ it immediately returns false. If the lengths match, it performs a byte‑by‑byte comparison of the underlying character sequences. Only when all characters compare equal does it return true. The comparison respects the character type and traits supplied in the template parameters.

@lstd::operator>=@k_ZStgeSt17basic_strin.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator>=@k_ZStgeSt17basic_strin.body: The operator takes two `basic_string_view` objects, compares their underlying buffers (typically via length and character-by‑character comparison), and returns `true` when all characters match and the lengths are equal, otherwise `false`.

@lstd::operator>@k_ZStgtRKNSt7__cxx1112b.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator>@k_ZStgtRKNSt7__cxx1112b.body:
It implements a comparison operator for `basic_string` types.  
When called, it takes two string references of matching `CharT`, `Traits`, and `Alloc` types and returns `true` if the two strings contain identical character sequences according to those traits and allocators, otherwise `false`. The implementation typically performs a straightforward element‑by‑element comparison (often using `std::equal` or an equivalent loop) to determine equality.

@lstd::operator>@k_ZStgtSt17basic_string.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator>@k_ZStgtSt17basic_string.body: The template returns a boolean indicating whether the first string view is lexicographically greater than the second. It performs a standard string comparison: first checking lengths and then element‑by‑element comparison using the character traits for the respective character type.

@lstd::operator|@k_ZStorSt13_Ios_Openmod.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::operator|@k_ZStorSt13_Ios_Openmod.body: The `operator|` function merges two `_Ios_Openmode` values into a single mode by performing a bitwise OR on their underlying flags, yielding a combined mode that can be passed to functions expecting a single `_Ios_Openmode`.

@lstd::optional::emplace@k_ZNSt8optional.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::emplace@k_ZNSt8optional.body: Constructs an object of type `_Tp` from perfectly‑forwarded arguments, returning a reference to that object. The function is enabled only when `_Tp` can be constructed with the supplied argument types, ensuring the call is SFINAE‑safe.

@lstd::optional::has_value@k_ZNKSt8optio.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::has_value@k_ZNKSt8optio.body: has_value() returns true when the underlying optional value is non‑empty, and false otherwise.

@lstd::optional::operator bool@k_ZNKSt8o.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator bool@k_ZNKSt8o.body: The `operator bool` function acts as a lightweight predicate that inspects the command‑execution flags supplied in an `Arguments` object and reports whether the standard‑output handling logic must be engaged. When invoked, it evaluates the `RunOutputStdOutVariable` and `RunOutputStdErrVariable` flags – which are passed into the `cmTryRunCommand` routine – and simply returns `true` if either of those flags is set, indicating that output should be captured; otherwise it returns `false`. This predicate is invoked in a handful of places, most notably when the surrounding code is deciding whether to redirect or ignore `stdout`/`stderr` streams during a `cmake` run.

@lstd::optional::operator*@k_ZNRSt8optio.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator*@k_ZNRSt8optio.body: The overload returns a reference to the internal type, enabling fluent chaining of the operation.

@lstd::optional::operator->@k_ZNSt8optio.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator->@k_ZNSt8optio.body: The overload returns a pointer to the wrapped object, allowing client code to access members directly (e.g., `wrapper->member`). It simply forwards the underlying pointer so that the wrapper behaves like a raw pointer for member‑access.

@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.body: The assignment operator takes an rvalue of `optional<cmTraceEnums::TraceOutputFormat>` and moves it into the optional instance, returning a reference to the same optional after the move. This allows using the operator to set or replace a value in a fluent manner while preserving move semantics.

@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.body: Assigns the supplied optional <cmCMakePresetsGraph::TraceEnableMode> value to the object and returns a reference to that optional.

@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.body: Moves an rvalue‑wrapped `optional<cmCMakePresetsGraph::ArchToolsetStrategy>` into the object, replacing any current value and returning a reference to the object for further chaining.

@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.body: Assigns a value from the right‑hand optional duration into the left‑hand optional, then returns a reference to that optional so the assignment can be chained.

@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.body:
The template declares an assignment operator for an `optional` type.  
It is enabled only when the supplied argument `_Up` is not the same type as the optional object itself, and when it can be converted to the underlying type.  
When invoked, the operator assigns the value into the optional’s storage and returns a reference to the optional for chaining.

@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::operator=@k_ZNSt8option.body: This overload assigns an `optional` to an empty state (`nullopt_t`), clearing its stored value and returning a reference to the same `optional` for chaining.

@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.body:
The `optional` template is a thin wrapper that represents a value that may or may not be present.  
It takes a type parameter (here `_Up`) and stores either a value of that type or an “empty” state.  
Typical usage constructs it with a value (`cm::optional<…>{ value }`) to indicate that the value is present, and an empty constructor to represent absence.  
The wrapper usually offers simple accessors (e.g., `has_value()` / `value()`) and is used throughout the code to keep optional semantics explicit and type‑safe.

@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.body: Creates an optional that contains no value.

@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.body: It checks whether a value is present and either returns that value or supplies a fallback, allowing callers to handle the absence of a value without propagating errors.

@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::optional@k_ZNSt8optiona.body: The `optional` function is a move‑constructor that takes an rvalue reference to an `optional<cmList>` and forwards that value to initialize the current instance. It preserves the move semantics of the underlying `optional` object and ensures that the original is left in a valid, but unspecified, state.

@lstd::optional::reset@k_ZNSt8optional5r.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::optional::reset@k_ZNSt8optional5r.body: The `reset()` function clears the internal state of the object, clearing any cached data, resetting counters and re‑initialising member variables to their defaults so that subsequent operations start from a known clean baseline.

@lstd::overflow_error::overflow_error@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::overflow_error::overflow_error@k_.body: The `overflow_error` function is a utility that signals an overflow condition. When invoked with a message string, it reports that an overflow has occurred—typically by logging the supplied message to the console or an error stream and then halting program execution (often via `abort()` or throwing an exception). This helper is used throughout the codebase wherever an operation would otherwise silently wrap or produce an incorrect result due to an arithmetic overflow.

@lstd::pair::pair@k_ZNSt4pairC1EOSt4pair.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::pair::pair@k_ZNSt4pairC1EOSt4pair.body: This constructor initializes a new pair by moving the two elements from an existing pair. It performs member‑wise moves of `first` and `second`, ensuring that the resulting pair contains moved‑into values without copying, and that the operation is noexcept when both element types are noexcept move‑constructible.

@lstd::pair::pair@k_ZNSt4pairC1EOTL0__OT.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::pair::pair@k_ZNSt4pairC1EOTL0__OT.body: This template simply constructs and returns an instance of `std::pair` (or the corresponding value‑type defined for a map implementation) from its two template arguments. It is used throughout the project to create the key/value objects that are inserted into various maps (`MapSourceFileFlags::value_type`, `Map_`, `MakefileMap::value_type`, etc.).

@lstd::queue::empty@k_ZNKSt5queue5emptyE.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::queue::empty@k_ZNKSt5queue5emptyE.body: `empty()` returns `true` when the container holds no elements; otherwise `false`.

@lstd::queue::front@k_ZNSt5queue5frontEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::queue::front@k_ZNSt5queue5frontEv.body: The function `front()` returns a reference to the first element in a container (typically a queue or deque). It does **not** remove that element; it merely provides access to the element that is currently at the front of the sequence. The returned reference is non‑modifiable unless the caller explicitly casts it to a non‑const type.

@lstd::queue::pop@k_ZNSt5queue3popEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::queue::pop@k_ZNSt5queue3popEv.body: The `pop()` routine removes the most recently added element from the underlying container, automatically advancing the internal index and clearing any stale references.

@lstd::queue::push@k_ZNSt5queue4pushERKN.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::queue::push@k_ZNSt5queue4pushERKN.body: push inserts the provided value into the underlying data structure, updating its internal state accordingly.

@lstd::queue::queue@k_ZNSt5queueC1Ev.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::queue::queue@k_ZNSt5queueC1Ev.body: This template defines a generic enqueue operation that accepts an element of any type and inserts it into an internal container, updating internal pointers or indices accordingly. @lstd::unique_ptr::unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10un.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unique_ptr::unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10un.body:
`unique_ptr` is a helper that creates a `std::unique_ptr` from a raw pointer.  
- **Template signature**  
  ```cpp
  template<class T, class Deleter = std::default_delete<T>>
  std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter> unique_ptr(T* ptr) noexcept;
  ```  
- **Behavior**  
  * Takes ownership of `ptr`.  
  * Transfers the pointer into a `unique_ptr` without copying the pointee.  
  * Requires that `ptr` is not `nullptr`; otherwise it returns an empty `unique_ptr`.  

- **Typical use‑case**  
  ```cpp
  auto p = unique_ptr(new Foo);
  // `p` now owns the `Foo` instance
  ```
