@lstd::unique_ptr::unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10un.body: It takes an rvalue reference to another `unique_ptr`, swaps the internal pointer to the new object, and leaves the source in a null state.

@lstd::unique_ptr::unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10un.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unique_ptr::unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10un.body: The `unique_ptr` helper template simply constructs a new object of the requested type and returns it wrapped in a `std::unique_ptr`. It’s used throughout the code to create objects in places such as `cmGlobalGeneratorFactory::Generate`, `cmNinjaTargetGenerator`, and `cmCryptoHash`.

@lstd::unique_ptr::~unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10u.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unique_ptr::~unique_ptr@k_ZNSt10u.body: The `~unique_ptr` helper simply creates and hands back a `std::unique_ptr` that owns the newly‑allocated object. It packages the allocation and ownership in a single call, so callers never need to write raw `new` followed by a `delete`‑capable wrapper—`unique_ptr` cleans itself up automatically.

@lstd::unordered_map::clear@k_ZNSt13unor.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::clear@k_ZNSt13unor.body: Resets internal buffers and data structures to an empty or default state, clearing any residual flags or stored values before the next operation.

@lstd::unordered_map::emplace@k_ZNSt13un.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::emplace@k_ZNSt13un.body: The emplace template performs an insertion into a container (typically a map or unordered_map) and returns a pair consisting of an iterator to the inserted (or found) element and a bool that reports whether the insertion actually took place. The return value signals success when the element wasn’t previously present; otherwise the iterator points to the existing element.

@lstd::unordered_map::end@k_ZNKSt13unord.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::end@k_ZNKSt13unord.body: Returning a read‑only iterator that represents the position after the final element, enabling read‑only traversal to the container’s end.

@lstd::unordered_map::end@k_ZNSt13unorde.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::end@k_ZNSt13unorde.body: The `end()` function returns an iterator pointing just past the last element of the container, serving as the sentinel in loop conditions and range‑based for loops.

@lstd::unordered_map::erase@k_ZNSt13unor.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::erase@k_ZNSt13unor.body: The function takes a key, deletes the corresponding entry from the underlying storage, and returns the number of elements that were removed (zero if the key was not present).

@lstd::unordered_map::find@k_ZNKSt13unor.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::find@k_ZNKSt13unor.body: The `find` member returns a constant iterator to the map entry whose key matches the supplied key. If no such key exists, it returns the map’s `end()` iterator, leaving the map unchanged. This allows callers to inspect or use the value without modifying the underlying container.

@lstd::unordered_map::find@k_ZNSt13unord.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::find@k_ZNSt13unord.body: The `find` function performs a lookup in the internal map structure. It accepts a key (passed by const reference) and returns an iterator pointing to the corresponding entry if it exists, or `end()` when the key is absent. The operation traverses the hash‑ or tree‑based map in expected `O(log n)` time and yields a lightweight reference to the stored value without copying it. This enables callers to inspect, modify, or erase the element only through the returned iterator.

@lstd::unordered_map::insert@k_ZNSt13uno.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::insert@k_ZNSt13uno.body:
The `insert` member performs the usual insertion operation: it attempts to insert the supplied value into the container, then returns a `std::pair<iterator, bool>`.  
The iterator points either to the newly inserted element (or the existing element if the value was already present), and the boolean flag tells whether a new element was actually inserted (`true`) or a duplicate was detected (`false`).

@lstd::unordered_map::operator[]@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::operator[]@k_ZNSt1.body: The `operator[]` takes a key (moved by `&&`), performs a lookup or inserts a default entry if the key is missing, and then returns a reference to the value stored under that key.

@lstd::unordered_map::operator[]@k_ZNSt1.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::operator[]@k_ZNSt1.body: The subscript operator returns a reference to the value corresponding to the supplied key. If the key is missing, the map will insert a new element with a default‑constructed value before returning the reference, enabling the caller to read or modify the entry in place.

@lstd::unordered_map::size@k_ZNKSt13unor.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_map::size@k_ZNKSt13unor.body: The function simply reports how many elements the container currently holds. It is marked const, so calling it cannot alter the object’s state.

@lstd::unordered_set::emplace@k_ZNSt13un.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_set::emplace@k_ZNSt13un.body: The `emplace` template forwards its arguments to a container‑specific inserter, yielding an iterator pointing to the newly inserted element and a flag that reports whether the insertion actually altered the container.

@lstd::unordered_set::end@k_ZNSt13unorde.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_set::end@k_ZNSt13unorde.body: The `end()` function returns an iterator that represents the past‑the‑last position of the current collection. In the codebase it is used as a boundary marker: the iterator returned by `end()` is compared against other iterators in `if` or `while` conditions to determine whether a loop has finished or whether an element exists. It is the canonical “end” sentinel for the internal containers (e.g., `Rules`, `GeneratedFiles`, `jDeps`, etc.) and is employed in the surrounding code to perform bounds checks, insertions, or look‑ups.

@lstd::unordered_set::find@k_ZNSt13unord.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_set::find@k_ZNSt13unord.body: The `find` member searches the internal map for an entry keyed by the provided `key_type`. It returns the iterator pointing to the matching element if present; otherwise it yields `end()` to signal absence.

@lstd::unordered_set::insert@k_ZNSt13uno.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_set::insert@k_ZNSt13uno.body: The member returns a `std::pair<iterator,bool>`; the iterator points to the element that was actually inserted or was already present, and the bool signals whether the insertion actually added a new element (true) or detected an existing key (false).

@lstd::unordered_set::unordered_set@k_ZN.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::unordered_set::unordered_set@k_ZN.body: Creates a hash‑based set that holds elements without ordering guarantees, efficiently deduplicating inputs and allowing rapid look‑ups, inserts, and deletions.

@lstd::vector::at@k_ZNKSt6vector2atEm.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::at@k_ZNKSt6vector2atEm.body: The `at` member simply returns a constant reference to the element stored at the requested position. It accepts a `size_type` index and forwards that index to the underlying container’s own `at` routine (which performs bounds checking). It is a `const` function, so callers may not modify the returned element and may use it in read‑only contexts throughout the code.

@lstd::vector::at@k_ZNSt6vector2atEm.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::at@k_ZNSt6vector2atEm.body: The function returns a reference to the element in the container located at the given logical position. It forwards the requested index to the internal storage array (or list) where that element is stored, and hands back that reference. This lets callers read or modify the value at that particular slot without copying the underlying data.

@lstd::vector::back@k_ZNKSt6vector4backE.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::back@k_ZNKSt6vector4backE.body: The `back()` member returns a constant reference to the list’s last element, letting callers read (but not modify) the final stored value. It is invoked in several parts of the code to fetch the last string in a `args` vector—for example, extracting the variable name of a command. Because it returns a reference, the caller must keep the underlying object alive; calling it on an empty list would be undefined behaviour.

@lstd::vector::back@k_ZNSt6vector4backEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::back@k_ZNSt6vector4backEv.body: The `back()` member simply returns a reference to the last element stored in the internal container (`Values`, `Processes`, `curl_ranges`, `Names`, etc.). It’s used in the code to fetch the most recently added item for further inspection or manipulation. No special logic is performed beyond that single return; callers typically rely on the container’s own `back()` semantics to guarantee that the container isn’t empty before invoking the method.

@lstd::vector::begin@k_ZNKSt6vector5begi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::begin@k_ZNKSt6vector5begi.body:
`begin()` returns a `const_iterator` pointing to the first element of the collection.  
Because it is declared `const`, the iterator is read‑only and cannot modify the underlying data.  
When the collection is empty, the returned iterator equals the container’s `end()` iterator.  
The function is typically invoked in algorithm calls such as `std::transform( …, *this->begin(), …)` or `std::any_of( …, *this->begin(), …)`.

@lstd::vector::begin@k_ZNSt6vector5begin.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::begin@k_ZNSt6vector5begin.body: Retrieves the iterator pointing to the very first element of the internal container, allowing callers to walk the sequence from the start onward.

@lstd::vector::cbegin@k_ZNKSt6vector6cbe.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::cbegin@k_ZNKSt6vector6cbe.body: `cbegin` is a const member function that returns a `const_iterator` to the first element of `Values`. It provides read‑only access to the container’s beginning, enabling callers to compute offsets or positions without altering the underlying sequence. In the code examples, it’s used to establish a reference point when calculating distances—e.g. `std::distance(this->Values.cbegin(), pos)`, `std::distance(this->Values.cbegin(), first)`, and `std::distance(this->Values.cbegin(), last)`—so the iterator returned by `cbegin()` serves as the origin for those distance computations.

@lstd::vector::cend@k_ZNKSt6vector4cendE.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::cend@k_ZNKSt6vector4cendE.body: It returns a const‐iterator that marks the position just beyond the final element of the internal container, allowing callers to treat that point as a sentinel when traversing or inserting without altering the underlying collection.

@lstd::vector::clear@k_ZNSt6vector5clear.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::clear@k_ZNSt6vector5clear.body: The `clear()` function resets the internal state of the object—empting any stored data and restoring default values so the instance is ready for a new operation.

@lstd::vector::crbegin@k_ZNKSt6vector7cr.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::crbegin@k_ZNKSt6vector7cr.body: The function returns a `const_reverse_iterator` that points to the element that would be first when the container is traversed in reverse order. This iterator can be used to iterate over the container from the last element back to the first one, without modifying the underlying data.

@lstd::vector::crend@k_ZNKSt6vector5cren.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::crend@k_ZNKSt6vector5cren.body: It returns a `const_reverse_iterator` positioned at the element after the first one in the container, allowing read‑only reverse traversal of `Values`.

@lstd::vector::data@k_ZNSt6vector4dataEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::data@k_ZNSt6vector4dataEv.body: The member function `data()` returns a pointer to the internal buffer that holds the object’s raw data. It is templated on the type `_Tp`; callers receive a (typically const-qualified) pointer to that buffer and use it for reading, argument parsing, buffer initialization, or text extraction. The function simply exposes the underlying array without copying, ensuring efficient access while preserving encapsulation of the internal storage.

@lstd::vector::emplace@k_ZNSt6vectorINSt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::emplace@k_ZNSt6vectorINSt.body: The `emplace` template is a helper that inserts an element into a container at a given position by forwarding the supplied constructor arguments. It accepts an iterator to the desired insertion point and a variadic pack of arguments, then constructs the element in‑place (typically via `std::forward`). The returned iterator points to the newly inserted element.

@lstd::vector::emplace_back@k_ZNSt6vecto.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::emplace_back@k_ZNSt6vecto.body: The emplace_back template forwards its arguments to an underlying emplace_back implementation, enabling in‑place construction of new elements into a container. It accepts forwarding references, forwarding them to the actual emplacement logic so that no unnecessary copies or moves are performed.

@lstd::vector::emplace_back@k_ZNSt6vecto.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::emplace_back@k_ZNSt6vecto.body: The template forwards a variadic pack of arguments to the underlying `emplace_back` helper, constructing and inserting an element in‑place into the target container. It then returns a reference to the newly inserted element.

@lstd::vector::empty@k_ZNKSt6vector5empt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::empty@k_ZNKSt6vector5empt.body: It’s a lightweight const accessor that simply reports whether the internal collection has any elements – it forwards the call to the underlying container’s `empty()` method and returns the same boolean value.

@lstd::vector::end@k_ZNKSt6vector3endEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::end@k_ZNKSt6vector3endEv.body: Returns a constant iterator positioned at the container’s end, allowing callers to identify when a loop or transformation has finished or to probe the presence of elements in the succeeding code sections.

@lstd::vector::end@k_ZNSt6vector3endEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::end@k_ZNSt6vector3endEv.body: The `end()` member simply returns an iterator that represents the container’s logical “end” point. In the surrounding code it’s used as the sentinel in `std::any_of` calls to terminate the search once the iterator reaches that sentinel.

@lstd::vector::erase@k_ZNSt6vector5erase.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::erase@k_ZNSt6vector5erase.body: Erases removes the element at the given iterator position from the container, updates the internal list, and returns an iterator that points to the element that followed the erased one (or to `end()` if the erased element was the last).

@lstd::vector::erase@k_ZNSt6vector5erase.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::erase@k_ZNSt6vector5erase.body: Removes the elements in the inclusive‑open range `[first,last)` of the list and returns an iterator pointing to the element that follows the removed range (or `end()` if the last element was erased). The operation runs in linear time proportional to the number of items erased and guarantees strong exception safety by performing the deallocation in a single pass.

@lstd::vector::front@k_ZNKSt6vector5fron.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::front@k_ZNKSt6vector5fron.body: The `front()` function returns a const reference to the first element in the container’s underlying collection. It’s a non‑modifying accessor that forwards the call to the internal `Values` collection (as seen in `cmList.h`) or to the argument vector in various command classes. In each usage the caller receives the first argument or value without copying or mutation, simply passing that reference to subsequent logic (e.g., for fetching a definition name or scope name).

@lstd::vector::front@k_ZNSt6vector5front.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::front@k_ZNSt6vector5front.body: front() returns the first element in the internal collection, exposing it by reference for callers to read or manipulate.

@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.body: The function `insert` takes a position (`const_iterator`) and an rvalue reference to a value (`value_type&&`), forwards that value to the underlying container’s `insert`, and returns an iterator pointing to the newly inserted element. It guarantees that the element is moved into the container without unnecessary copies and that the returned iterator is valid after insertion.

@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.body: The function takes an iterator pointing to a location inside the container and a const reference to the value to be inserted. It inserts the value before that position in the underlying sequence and returns an iterator that refers directly to the newly inserted element.

@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.body: The function inserts a range of values from the given initializer‑list into the container at the position specified by the preceding iterator. After the insertion it returns an iterator that points to the first element that was inserted.

@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.body: The `insert` template takes a position iterator, a beginning iterator, and an ending iterator. It inserts the elements in the range `[first, last)` at the position indicated by the first argument, returning an iterator pointing to the first element that was inserted.

@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vector6inse.body: Inserts a value at a specified position in the container and returns an iterator that points to the newly inserted element.

@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vectorINSt7.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::insert@k_ZNSt6vectorINSt7.body: The template inserts a range of elements into a collection at the position specified by a `const_iterator`. It returns an iterator pointing to the last element inserted, or the end iterator if the range is empty. The function accepts any input iterator range and forwards the elements into the underlying container, preserving the order of the input sequence.

@lstd::vector::operator=@k_ZNSt6vectoraS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::operator=@k_ZNSt6vectoraS.body: Moves the contents of a temporary vector into this instance (by moving its resources), leaving the source in a valid but unspecified state and returning a reference to the current vector.

@lstd::vector::operator=@k_ZNSt6vectoraS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::operator=@k_ZNSt6vectoraS.body: Assigns a new vector from the right‑hand side, copying its elements, size, and capacity while preserving exception safety and handling self‑assignment correctly.

@lstd::vector::operator=@k_ZNSt6vectoraS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::operator=@k_ZNSt6vectoraS.body: Copies elements from the initializer list into the vector, replacing current contents atomically; it constructs a temporary vector and swaps, guaranteeing strong exception safety.

@lstd::vector::operator[]@k_ZNKSt6vector.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::operator[]@k_ZNKSt6vector.body: This operator returns a const reference to the element at the supplied index, guaranteeing that the caller cannot modify the underlying container.

@lstd::vector::operator[]@k_ZNSt6vectorI.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::operator[]@k_ZNSt6vectorI.body: operator[] returns a reference to the element at the specified index, enabling read‑write access into the underlying container.

@lstd::vector::operator[]@k_ZNSt6vectori.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::operator[]@k_ZNSt6vectori.body: Returns a reference to the element at the given index, allowing the caller to read or modify that element. The operator is typically defined in a container class that stores elements in a contiguous array. It usually performs no bounds‑checking unless the implementation explicitly adds it, so passing an out‑of‑range index results in undefined behaviour (often a crash or memory overwrite). The return type is the container’s element reference type, which can be used in assignment expressions (e.g. `c[i] = 5;`). The operator is a constant‑time (O(1)) access assuming the underlying storage is an array or vector‑like container. In multi‑threaded contexts, the function should not modify any shared state unless it is marked `noexcept`; otherwise concurrent modifications may need external synchronization.

@lstd::vector::pop_back@k_ZNSt6vector8po.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::pop_back@k_ZNSt6vector8po.body: This method removes the element at the back of the collection, decrementing the size counter and updating any internal linkage so that the container reflects the loss of its most recently added item.

@lstd::vector::push_back@k_ZNSt6vector9p.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::push_back@k_ZNSt6vector9p.body: The `push_back` function accepts an rvalue reference of type `value_type`. It constructs a new element in place‑on the internal container (typically a vector‑like structure) and appends it, moving the supplied value into the new node without copying. The operation runs in amortised constant time, typically pushing the element onto the end of the sequence.

@lstd::vector::push_back@k_ZNSt6vector9p.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::push_back@k_ZNSt6vector9p.body: The function takes a value by const reference and appends it to the underlying sequence, preserving ownership semantics while avoiding copies of the argument. It returns immediately after insertion.

@lstd::vector::rbegin@k_ZNKSt6vector6rbe.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::rbegin@k_ZNKSt6vector6rbe.body: The `rbegin()` member returns a `const_reverse_iterator` that points to the final element of the underlying container, allowing read‑only reverse traversal without modifying the collection. It is invoked in `cmList.h` to expose the list’s reverse iterator, and in `cmComputeLinkDepends.cxx` to iterate a dependent list in descending order.

@lstd::vector::rbegin@k_ZNSt6vector6rbeg.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::rbegin@k_ZNSt6vector6rbeg.body: The `rbegin` member function returns a `reverse_iterator` positioned at the first element of the container, allowing iteration in reverse order.

@lstd::vector::rend@k_ZNKSt6vector4rendE.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::rend@k_ZNKSt6vector4rendE.body: Returns a const reverse iterator that represents the logical “end” of a reverse traversal of the underlying container.

@lstd::vector::rend@k_ZNSt6vector4rendEv.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::rend@k_ZNSt6vector4rendEv.body:
Returns a reverse iterator that points just past the last element of the container.  
The returned iterator represents the logical “end” position when traversing the collection in reverse order, and is used throughout the code to delimit reverse‑range loops or to obtain the end of a reverse view (`rbegin()` … `rend()`).

@lstd::vector::reserve@k_ZNSt6vector7res.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::reserve@k_ZNSt6vector7res.body: The reserve function takes a size argument and adjusts the container’s internal allocation so that a future number of elements can be stored without triggering a reallocation. It typically enlarges the internal buffer to at least the requested amount or throws an exception if allocation fails.

@lstd::vector::resize@k_ZNSt6vector6resi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::resize@k_ZNSt6vector6resi.body: Resizes the internal data structure to the requested size, reallocating or truncating as necessary while preserving existing elements where possible.

@lstd::vector::resize@k_ZNSt6vector6resi.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::resize@k_ZNSt6vector6resi.body: The `resize` function changes the internal storage to the requested size. It accepts a target size (`size_type`) and a value (`value_type`) that is used to initialize any new elements when the container expands. During shrinking, elements beyond the new size are destroyed, while expanding triggers reallocation that preserves existing elements and fills the newly allocated slots with the provided value. The operation is exception‑safe: if allocation fails, the original container state remains untouched.

@lstd::vector::size@k_ZNKSt6vector4sizeE.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::size@k_ZNKSt6vector4sizeE.body: The function returns the count of elements in the collection, typically by accessing an internal counter or by summing the sizes of any sub‑collections it holds. It is marked const because calling it does not modify the object’s state, so callers can safely invoke it without side effects.

@lstd::vector::swap@k_ZNSt6vector4swapER.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::swap@k_ZNSt6vector4swapER.body: When invoked, `vector::swap` exchanges the entire storage of the current vector with that of another vector of the same type, leaving both objects in a valid state. The operation is effectively constant‑time, merely swapping internal pointers and sizes; no element‑level copying occurs. It guarantees strong exception safety (nothing is destroyed), and is marked `noexcept`.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1EOS.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1EOS.body: Creates a new vector by taking ownership of another vector’s elements, leaving the source in an unspecified but valid state.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1ERK.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1ERK.body: Creates a new vector by copying all elements from the supplied vector, allocating the same amount of storage and copying each element in order, resulting in an identical logical container.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1ESt.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1ESt.body: The public `vector` constructor you’re looking at simply creates a dynamic array of the specified type. It accepts an `initializer_list` of values and an allocator (which defaults to `std::allocator_traits<T>::type`). The constructor copies each list element into the internal storage in the order given, allocating enough space upfront. When you pass a list of values it will build a vector holding those values in sequence, ready for random‑index access, push_back, pop_back, and all the usual vector operations.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1ETL.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1ETL.body: The `vector` function template constructs and returns a standard `std::vector` by copying the elements in the range `[first, last)` supplied by the two `InputIterator` arguments, using the supplied `allocator_type` to allocate the internal storage. It essentially forwards those iterators and the allocator to the `std::vector` constructor, producing a vector that contains exactly the elements found in that range.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1EmR.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1EmR.body: Creates a vector of the specified size, allocating its storage through the supplied allocator.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1EmR.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1EmR.body: Creates a vector of the requested size, filling every element with the supplied value while allocating memory through the given allocator.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1Ev.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorC1Ev.body: Returns a vector of strings, usually populated from file‑path or component names. The function is called from various generator files to provide a list of strings (often file names or identifiers) that downstream code consumes.

@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorIbT_E.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::vector@k_ZNSt6vectorIbT_E.body: Allocates memory for the requested number of elements, optionally value‑initializes them according to the passed flag, and uses the supplied allocator for the underlying memory management.

@lstd::vector::~vector@k_ZNSt6vectorD1Ev.author: AI Short Overview
@lstd::vector::~vector@k_ZNSt6vectorD1Ev.body: The `~vector()` function is the class destructor. It runs automatically when an instance of `vector` goes out of scope, releasing any dynamic memory and other resources that were allocated by the container.

@lstpcpy@kstpcpy.author: AI Short Overview
@lstpcpy@kstpcpy.body: Copies the contents of the source string into a pre‑allocated destination buffer (`dest`) until the terminating `'\0'`, and then returns a pointer that points just past the last copied character. The function is used in the parser modules (`cmExprParser.cxx`, `cmFortranParser.cxx`, `cmDependsJavaParser.cxx`) to quickly compute the offset of the string within the temporary buffer (`yyres`) and return that offset as an integer.

@lstrcmp@kstrcmp.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrcmp@kstrcmp.body: `strcmp` performs a byte‑wise comparison of two null‑terminated character arrays and returns an integer: negative if the first string precedes the second lexicographically, zero if they are equal, and positive if the first follows the second. It is typically used in sorting and equality checks where string ordering matters.

@lstrftime@kstrftime.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrftime@kstrftime.body: `strftime` takes a destination buffer, its size, a format string, and a `tm` pointer, then writes a formatted date‑time string into that buffer according to the format specifiers. It returns the number of characters written (or `-1` on failure). The function performs the usual string‑formation routine: it parses the format string, substitutes the appropriate date/time fields from the supplied `tm` structure, and copies the result into the supplied buffer. It stops if the buffer size would be exceeded, guaranteeing no overflow.

@lstrlen@kstrlen.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrlen@kstrlen.body: The `strlen` routine accepts a pointer to a null‑terminated character array and returns the number of bytes preceding the terminator. It performs a simple linear scan, incrementing a counter until it encounters `'\0'`. The helper is used in several parser stages to compute buffer sizes, e.g. the offsets used in `yy_scan_bytes` calls. The implementation assumes a valid C‑string; passing a `nullptr` will immediately return 0.

@lstrncmp@kstrncmp.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrncmp@kstrncmp.body: strncmp compares up to a specified length of two strings and returns an integer indicating lexical ordering: < 0 if the first string precedes, 0 if equal, > 0 otherwise. It’s employed to test substring equality in the shown code paths.

@lstrncpy@kstrncpy.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrncpy@kstrncpy.body: `strncpy` copies at most `n` characters from a source string into a destination buffer, guaranteeing the destination is null‑terminated. It writes up to `n` bytes (including the terminating `'\0'` if space permits) and returns the destination pointer. It’s used for bounded copying, e.g. copying partial strings or copying into pre‑allocated buffers without overrunning the buffer.

@lstrtol@kstrtol.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrtol@kstrtol.body: `strtol` reads a C‑style string and converts its numeric prefix into a `long` value. It accepts the string to parse, a pointer-to‑pointer that will receive the address of the first character that was not consumed during the conversion, and the numeric base (e.g., 10 for decimal). The function scans the string until it encounters a character that cannot be part of a number in the given base, writes that position into the supplied pointer, and returns the parsed long value. If no digits are found, it returns 0 and leaves the end pointer pointing at the original start.

@lstrtoul@kstrtoul.author: AI Short Overview
@lstrtoul@kstrtoul.body: `strtoul` parses a null‑terminated C‑string into an unsigned long, optionally recording where parsing stopped in the supplied `char**` argument. The third argument selects the radix (e.g., 10 for decimal, 16 for hexadecimal). It returns the converted value or zero when no digits were found, and writes a pointer to the first non‑digit into the `endp` argument (which may be `nullptr`). The routine is a thin wrapper around the standard library’s `strtoul()`/`strtoul_l()` and is used throughout the code to read numeric values from buffers and buffers that may or may not contain a terminating null‑byte.

@lswap@k_Z4swapR11cmCMakePathS0_@f./Sour.author: AI Short Overview
@lswap@k_Z4swapR11cmCMakePathS0_@f./Sour.body: The function simply forwards a call to the member `swap` method of `cmCMakePath`, swapping the contents of the two passed objects. It’s marked `inline` and `noexcept` to avoid copying and provide strong exception safety.

@ltm::operator=@k_ZN2tmaSERKS_.author: AI Short Overview
@ltm::operator=@k_ZN2tmaSERKS_.body: The copy‑assignment operator copies every member of the right‑hand‐side `tm` into the current object, guarding against self‑assignment (by first checking if the addresses differ before copying). It then returns a reference to `*this` so that chained assignments can be used in code.

@ltm::tm@k_ZN2tmC1Ev.author: AI Short Overview
@ltm::tm@k_ZN2tmC1Ev.body: This public entry point delegates internal logic, coordinating the needed sub‑components to achieve the routine’s goal.

@ltoupper@ktoupper.author: AI Short Overview
@ltoupper@ktoupper.body: The `toupper` routine is a tiny helper that accepts an integer code‑point (typically a `char` value) and returns the same code point if it is already an uppercase alphabetic byte; otherwise it maps the lower‑case letter to its capital counterpart. It is essentially a small wrapper over the standard `toupper` logic, handling only the ASCII alphabetic range, and it never mutates any global state. The calls in the source files show it being inlined in several “::*toupper” contexts, hinting at the function being a lightweight, non‑virtualized shim used to keep the upper‑case conversion logic isolated from the rest of the code base.

@ltzset@ktzset.author: AI Short Overview
@ltzset@ktzset.body: Sets the system timezone variable (e.g. `TZ`) to the value configured in the program’s environment, ensuring subsequent date‑time calls use that zone.

@luv_buf_init@kuv_buf_init.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_buf_init@kuv_buf_init.body: The `uv_buf_init` routine builds a buffer descriptor around the supplied raw data pointer and length: it returns a `uv_buf_t` instance whose `data` field points to the supplied buffer and whose `size` field records the provided size, enabling the rest of the system to treat that block uniformly as a continuous byte sequence.

@luv_buf_t::operator=@k_ZN8uv_buf_taSEOS.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_buf_t::operator=@k_ZN8uv_buf_taSEOS.body: The `operator=` function takes an rvalue reference to a `uv_buf_t` and moves its contents into the current instance, replacing the old buffer and returning a reference to the modified object.

@luv_cpumask_size@kuv_cpumask_size.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_cpumask_size@kuv_cpumask_size.body:
The `uv_cpumask_size()` function reports the number of logical processors that the current process is allowed to use.  
It queries the system’s CPU topology (for example via `sched_getaffinity()` or similar) and returns the count of bits that must be allocated in a CPU‑mask bitset. The returned value is used to size a vector that will hold one bit per CPU, e.g. `cpumask.resize(uv_cpumask_size(), 0)`.

@luv_fs_req_cleanup@kuv_fs_req_cleanup.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_fs_req_cleanup@kuv_fs_req_cleanup.body: The routine releases all resources tied to a pending file‑system request: it frees any allocated buffers, closes the underlying file descriptor (if still open), and clears the request’s internal state so that it can be safely discarded or reused.

@luv_fs_s::uv_fs_s@k_ZN7uv_fs_sC1Ev.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_fs_s::uv_fs_s@k_ZN7uv_fs_sC1Ev.body: uv_fs_s is a public helper that orchestrates an internal file‑system operation. It accepts a request descriptor, dispatches the proper low‑level I/O routine, and returns the resulting status or content through a uniform, error‑checked API channel.

@luv_fs_stat@kuv_fs_stat.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_fs_stat@kuv_fs_stat.body: uv_fs_stat schedules an asynchronous stat operation on a supplied path. It takes a loop, a task descriptor, the path string, and a callback, returning immediately; the callback is invoked with the resulting file statistics once the operation completes.

@luv_gettimeofday@kuv_gettimeofday.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_gettimeofday@kuv_gettimeofday.body: Retrieves the current wall‑clock time into a `uv_timeval64_t` structure (seconds + nanoseconds since epoch) and returns 0 on success or a negative error code on failure.

@luv_pipe_open@kuv_pipe_open.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_pipe_open@kuv_pipe_open.body: The function `uv_pipe_open` takes a pointer to a `uv_pipe_t` and a file descriptor, initializes the pipe handle for the event loop, and returns an error code indicating success or failure.

@luv_process_kill@kuv_process_kill.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_process_kill@kuv_process_kill.body: This routine terminates a running UV process. It accepts a pointer to the process structure and an integer status code that is passed to the process’ exit routine. On success it returns 0; on failure it returns a negative error code. The function also performs any necessary cleanup of file descriptors and other resources owned by the process before it exits.

@luv_process_options_s::uv_process_optio.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_process_options_s::uv_process_optio.body: The `uv_process_options_s` routine is the single public entry point that gathers and normalises the options needed by the UV processing chain. It instantiates a `uv_process_options_t` instance, applies any default values or user‑supplied overrides, and performs validation before handing the options off to the downstream processing stages.

@luv_process_options_s::~uv_process_opti.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_process_options_s::~uv_process_opti.body: The ~uv_process_options_s function parses and normalizes configuration flags before a UV build. It reads an options table, validates required fields, normalizes values (e.g., expanding aliases or defaults), and injects defaults for any missing entries. It also merges overlapping options from multiple sources (CLI, config file, env vars) and emits diagnostic warnings for unsupported or conflicting settings. This pre‑validation step guarantees later phases receive a consistent, canonical options object that’s safe to use across the UV processing pipeline.

@luv_read_start@kuv_read_start.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_read_start@kuv_read_start.body: The `uv_read_start` helper registers the allocation and read callbacks for a given `uv_stream_t` instance, enabling the library to start pulling data from the stream. It returns an integer status indicating success or failure of the initiation.

@luv_run@kuv_run.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_run@kuv_run.body: uv_run starts the event loop on the supplied uv_loop_t instance. It processes queued callbacks until the loop is stopped and returns 0 on success (or a non‑zero error code). It expects the loop to have been initialized; the run mode argument controls whether the call blocks or performs a single iteration.

@luv_stdio_container_s::operator=@k_ZN20.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_stdio_container_s::operator=@k_ZN20.body: Assigns a temporary instance into the current object, moving all internal fields (e.g., file descriptors, buffers). It then returns the modified object by reference, allowing chained assignments and ensuring the source is left in a valid, empty‑state.

@luv_stdio_container_s::operator=@k_ZN20.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_stdio_container_s::operator=@k_ZN20.body: It performs a copy‑assignment: the left‑hand operand receives the values of every member of the right‑hand operand, then returns the left operand (by reference) so that callers can chain assignments.

@luv_stdio_container_s::uv_stdio_contain.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_stdio_container_s::uv_stdio_contain.body: The `uv_stdio_container_s` function constructs a lightweight container that encapsulates the interaction with standard streams inside a libuv loop, automatically handling the read/write events and buffering until the underlying file descriptor signals readiness.

@luv_strerror@kuv_strerror.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_strerror@kuv_strerror.body: The function maps an integer error code to a readable message from a static table and returns that message as a `const char*`.

@luv_timer_stop@kuv_timer_stop.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_timer_stop@kuv_timer_stop.body: uv_timer_stop stops a running timer. It receives a pointer to a uv_timer_t instance and returns an int status code (0 for success, non‑zero for error). It cancels any pending callbacks and releases resources associated with that timer.

@luv_timeval64_t::uv_timeval64_t@k_ZN14u.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_timeval64_t::uv_timeval64_t@k_ZN14u.body: The uv_timeval64_t function creates and returns a 64‑bit time representation: it takes a Unix‑epoch value (seconds) and a nanosecond offset, packs them into the internal uv_timeval64_t structure, and provides this value for subsequent timestamp handling.

@luv_translate_sys_error@kuv_translate_s.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_translate_sys_error@kuv_translate_s.body: `uv_translate_sys_error` converts a POSIX `errno` value into the library’s internal error code, returning that mapped value.

@luv_unref@kuv_unref.author: AI Short Overview
@luv_unref@kuv_unref.body: Removes a reference from a UV handle; once the count reaches zero the underlying resource is released and the handle’s memory freed.

@lwclrtoeol@kwclrtoeol.author: AI Short Overview
@lwclrtoeol@kwclrtoeol.body: This routine clears the current line of a `WINDOW` from the current column to the right margin. It writes space characters in that region and updates the display buffer, leaving any content beyond the margin untouched.

@lwcstombs@kwcstombs.author: AI Short Overview
@lwcstombs@kwcstombs.body: `wcstombs` converts a sequence of wide‑characters (`wchar_t*`) into a multibyte string written into the supplied buffer. It returns the number of bytes written (or `SIZE_MAX` on error) and can truncate the output to the supplied length (`n`). The routine is typically used in the `EncodingC` module to copy a string from a wide‑character representation into a narrow buffer, ensuring proper handling of null terminators and buffer overruns.

@lwgetch@kwgetch.author: AI Short Overview
@lwgetch@kwgetch.body: `wgetch` extracts the next key event from a given `WINDOW` instance and returns its integer code. It’s called throughout the application wherever key codes need to be read—particularly in string widgets and form handlers—so the routine must be fast and side‑effect‑free, always delivering the code the calling context expects.

@lwrefresh@kwrefresh.author: AI Short Overview
@lwrefresh@kwrefresh.body: The `wrefresh` routine accepts a `WINDOW*` argument, performs the internal steps to repaint or update the window’s contents (typically copying the back‑buffer to the display, clearing the dirty flag, and triggering a redraw of any visible elements), and returns an integer status code (0 for success, non‑zero for failure).

@lwtouchln@kwtouchln.author: AI Short Overview
@lwtouchln@kwtouchln.body: Updates a window’s touch line to the supplied coordinates and flag, adjusting the window’s internal state accordingly.

@lyy_fatal_error@k_ZL14yy_fatal_errorPKc.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_fatal_error@k_ZL14yy_fatal_errorPKc.body: The routine quietly casts the supplied scanner pointer to its internal structure type—though the resulting pointer is unused—then writes the supplied message to standard‑error and immediately terminates the process with the predefined failure exit code.

@lyy_get_next_buffer@k_ZL18yy_get_next_b.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_get_next_buffer@k_ZL18yy_get_next_b.body: This function refills the scanner’s circular buffer: it first preserves any trailing characters that were not consumed, moves them to the buffer start, then attempts to read more input from the underlying stream. If the buffer is already full or the underlying read yields no more data, it marks an EOF condition and returns the appropriate status code. It also resizes the buffer when needed and updates the internal pointers so the scanner can continue consuming characters.

@lyy_get_previous_state@k_ZL21yy_get_pre.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_get_previous_state@k_ZL21yy_get_pre.body: The routine walks forward from the current text pointer, consulting the transition tables until no more transition exists. During that walk it records the most recent accepted state and its position, then finally returns the terminal state reached.

@lyy_init_globals@k_ZL15yy_init_globalsP.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_init_globals@k_ZL15yy_init_globalsP.body: The function zero‑initializes the `yyg` context struct fields, sets the input/output streams to `stdin`/`stdout` when `YY_STDINIT` is defined (otherwise leaves them NULL), and returns 0.

@lyy_reduce_print@k_ZL15yy_reduce_printP.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_reduce_print@k_ZL15yy_reduce_printP.body: The routine emits a trace of a grammar reduction: it prints the rule number and its source‑code line, then iterates over the right‑hand side symbols that will be popped from the parser stack, printing each symbol’s type/value via a helper formatter. This tracing aid is only active when debugging is enabled, allowing developers to see which symbols were consumed during a reduction step.

@lyy_stack_print@k_ZL14yy_stack_printPaS.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_stack_print@k_ZL14yy_stack_printPaS.body: The function walks the state chain from the supplied bottom pointer up to the top pointer, printing each integer value stored in the state struct. It uses the `YYFPRINTF` macro to send the output to `stderr`. The loop increments the pointer until it passes the top element, emitting a space‑separated list of state values terminated by a newline.

@lyy_symbol_print@k_ZL15yy_symbol_printP.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_symbol_print@k_ZL15yy_symbol_printP.body: It writes a formatted description of a grammar symbol to the supplied stream. The routine first prints the token/non‑terminal label (“token” or “nterm”) followed by the symbol’s name, then delegates to `yy_symbol_value_print` to render the symbol’s value, and finally terminates the output with a closing parenthesis.

@lyy_symbol_value_print@k_ZL21yy_symbol_.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_symbol_value_print@k_ZL21yy_symbol_.body: The function receives a file stream, a symbol kind, a pointer to a value, and a scanner context. It immediately guards against a null value pointer and then, via the internal macros, would dispatch printing logic based on the symbol kind. The current body only contains guard and macro scaffolding, but the intent is to output a formatted representation of the value to the supplied stream.

@lyy_syntax_error_arguments@k_ZL25yy_syn.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_syntax_error_arguments@k_ZL25yy_syn.body: The function collects the token that triggered a syntax error and, if requested, fills a supplied array with that token followed by a list of tokens that would have been accepted at that point. It first records the offending token, then queries the parser context for all expected tokens, appending them to the array and returning the total count of entries.

@lyy_syntax_error_arguments@k_ZL25yy_syn.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_syntax_error_arguments@k_ZL25yy_syn.body: The routine gathers the offending token and the list of tokens that could have been accepted at that point. If the parser has a look‑ahead token (`yyctx->yytoken` not equal to `YYSYMBOL_YYEMPTY`), the function first copies that token into the supplied array. It then calls `yypcontext_expected_tokens` to enumerate the tokens that would be accepted in the current state, appending them to the array. The number of tokens added is returned; if the call to `yypcontext_expected_tokens` runs out of memory, the routine returns `YYENOMEM`. If no look‑ahead exists, it simply reports zero.

@lyy_try_NUL_trans@k_ZL16yy_try_NUL_tran.author: AI Short Overview
@lyy_try_NUL_trans@k_ZL16yy_try_NUL_tran.body: The function updates the current parsing state, sets the accept‑position when a state is accepted, follows the transition table until a match is found, and finally returns 0 if the transition reaches a jam state (state 31) or the new state index otherwise.

@lyydestruct@k_ZL10yydestructPKc15yysymb.author: AI Short Overview
@lyydestruct@k_ZL10yydestructPKc15yysymb.body: The `yydestruct` routine cleans up a symbol’s string buffer. It first prints the symbol via `YY_SYMBOL_PRINT` and then, based on the `yykind` value, executes a `switch` that frees the `string` member when the kind matches `YYSYMBOL_STRING`, `YYSYMBOL_WORD`, or `YYSYMBOL_CPP_INCLUDE_ANGLE`. The `YY_IGNORE_MAYBE_UNINITIALIZED_*` wrappers protect against uninitialized memory usage during the cleanup.

@lyydestruct@k_ZL10yydestructPKc15yysymb.author: AI Short Overview
@lyydestruct@k_ZL10yydestructPKc15yysymb.body: The function `yydestruct` is a static helper invoked during the parser’s cleanup phase. It receives a message string, a symbol kind enum value, a pointer to the semantic value to be discarded, and a scanner object. The routine first normalizes the message string to a default of “Deleting” when none is supplied. It then delegates the actual reporting to the `YY_SYMBOL_PRINT` macro, feeding it the message, kind, value pointer, and the location pointer (`yylocationp`). Finally, it invokes the `YY_IGNORE_MAYBE_UNINITIALIZED_*` macros to silence any compiler warnings about unused parameters (`yykind`). The body does no other work beyond these diagnostics‑or‑suppressing steps.

@lyyguts_t::yyguts_t@k_ZN8yyguts_tC1EOS_.author: AI Short Overview
@lyyguts_t::yyguts_t@k_ZN8yyguts_tC1EOS_.body: It’s a move‑style constructor that takes an rvalue reference to a yyguts_t instance and returns a fresh copy, used throughout the lexer modules to carry a small set of lexical state values that the various lexer implementations share.

@lyyguts_t::yyguts_t@k_ZN8yyguts_tC1ERKS.author: AI Short Overview
@lyyguts_t::yyguts_t@k_ZN8yyguts_tC1ERKS.body: The constructor creates a new `yyguts_t` instance by copying the internal state from the supplied object. All member variables are duplicated so that the new instance starts with the same configuration as the source.

@lyyguts_t::yyguts_t@k_ZN8yyguts_tC1Ev.author: AI Short Overview
@lyyguts_t::yyguts_t@k_ZN8yyguts_tC1Ev.body: The `yyguts_t()` routine constructs and returns a `yyguts_t` structure that holds the internal state required by the various lexer modules. It initializes the fields with the default values needed for the lexers to operate correctly.

@lyypcontext_expected_tokens@k_ZL26yypco.author: AI Short Overview
@lyypcontext_expected_tokens@k_ZL26yypco.body:
The function computes how many input token kinds can legally follow the current parser state.  
It checks the parsing table for the state given in `yyctx`, counts each token that is neither an error nor the special empty symbol, and optionally records those token kinds in the supplied `yyarg` array up to `yyargn`. The return value is the total number of such tokens (zero if none).

@lyypcontext_expected_tokens@k_ZL26yypco.author: AI Short Overview
@lyypcontext_expected_tokens@k_ZL26yypco.body: The routine scans the action table for the current parser state, collects the token kinds that would lead to a non‑error transition, and writes those token identifiers into the supplied array. It returns the number of tokens found (or 0 if none). If no tokens are found and an array pointer is supplied, it writes the special “empty” token marker as the single result. The function relies on the global tables `yypact`, `yycheck`, `yytname`, and `yytable` to perform its lookup.

@lyysymbol_name@k_ZL13yysymbol_name15yys.author: AI Short Overview
@lyysymbol_name@k_ZL13yysymbol_name15yys.body: The function looks up the supplied enumeration value in a static string‑array and returns the corresponding C‑string; it’s a thin wrapper that simply returns `yytname[yysymbol]`.

@lyysymbol_name@k_ZL13yysymbol_name15yys.author: AI Short Overview
@lyysymbol_name@k_ZL13yysymbol_name15yys.body: This function retrieves the name string for a given symbol kind by indexing a static array of names with the enum value, returning a pointer to that constant string.

@lyysyntax_error@k_ZL14yysyntax_errorPlP.author: AI Short Overview
@lyysyntax_error@k_ZL14yysyntax_errorPlP.body: The function builds a human‑readable syntax‑error message. It first counts how many unexpected/expected tokens are to be reported, then picks an appropriate format string from a small table of predefined patterns. Next it computes the exact buffer size required for that message, enlarging the supplied allocation size if necessary, and finally it writes the formatted string into the caller’s buffer—doing the string substitution manually rather than using a variadic helper, so that no external name collision occurs.

@lyysyntax_error@k_ZL14yysyntax_errorPlP.author: AI Short Overview
@lyysyntax_error@k_ZL14yysyntax_errorPlP.body: The routine assembles a single‑string error message for a syntax error. It first determines how many tokens were involved (unexpected and expected), selects the matching format template, then calculates the total length needed for the final string. If the supplied buffer is too small, it signals the shortage and returns –1; otherwise it writes the formatted message into the buffer and returns 0.

@lyytnamerr@k_ZL9yytnamerrPcPKc@p@l./Sou.author: AI Short Overview
@lyytnamerr@k_ZL9yytnamerrPcPKc@p@l./Sou.body: The routine removes the outer quotation marks of a string literal, unescapes any escaped backslashes, and writes the cleaned characters into a supplied buffer, finally returning the number of characters written.

@lyytnamerr@k_ZL9yytnamerrPcPKc@p@l./Sou.author: AI Short Overview
@lyytnamerr@k_ZL9yytnamerrPcPKc@p@l./Sou.body: The `yytnamerr` routine decodes a quoted string literal. It walks the source buffer, copying characters into the output buffer while recognizing escape sequences (`\\` → literal backslash, `\'` and `,` treated literally, and a trailing `"` terminates the copy). If the input string is already escaped the function simply returns its length; otherwise it parses and writes the unescaped form into the supplied buffer, returning the resulting length. It also protects against unterminated strings by aborting the copy when a closing quote is not found.
